posts.description: Toys for language development: why a toy that repeats is a mirror, what research says about back-and-forth talk, and how screens and speakers compare.
posts.author: Kheelona
posts.heroAlt: A laughing girl with a long braid holds a yellow paper crown on her head, beside a low table scattered with crayons and paper scraps.

content.text: Walk down a toy aisle and the talking toys line up: phones with phrase buttons, dolls with a handful of sentences, plush toys that sing when squeezed, a cactus that repeats whatever your child says.
They all talk. Listening is a different thing.
A toy that talks is not a toy that listens
A toy that talks plays sounds at your child: a recorded phrase, a song, or your child’s own words played back. A toy that listens has to understand what your child said, and answer it.

A toy that repeats is a mirror. It can be funny, but it can’t answer a question, and it never asks one of its own. A toy with a handful of sentences has nothing new to say once your child has heard them all.
What helps language development?

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth “serve and return” exchanges between a young child and a caring adult help build and strengthen neural connections in the child’s brain. They also support the early language and social skills that later, more complex thinking builds on.[^1]

In a 2018 study of 36 children aged 4 to 6, children who had more back-and-forth conversational turns with adults showed more activity in Broca’s area, a language region of the brain, while listening to a story. The number of adult words they heard showed no such link. The study shows a link, not cause and effect.[^2]
Both are about adults talking with children; neither tested a toy.[^1][^2] So ask one thing of any toy: will it get your child talking, and give the two of you more to talk about?
Screens, speakers and talking toys: how do they compare?
Videos and cartoons

A video plays on whether your child answers or not. The American Academy of Pediatrics asks parents to watch with their children and help them understand what they are seeing.[^3] The talking about it is the part that’s yours.
Smart speakers
A smart speaker answers questions, which a button toy can’t. Before your child talks to one alone, check its settings: what it can search, what it can play, and what it keeps of your child’s voice.
Talking toys that repeat or play phrases
They can’t answer a question they’ve never heard, so a conversation stops after one line. Keep them for the giggle, and do the talking yourself.
Toys that use AI to answer

Some newer toys use AI to understand your child and reply. They raise questions a button toy never did: when the microphone is on, where your child’s voice goes, and whether you can read every conversation. Before one comes home, read
What to look for in a safe AI toy
A short checklist for any talking toy
Does it reply, or only repeat?
Does it ask your child something back, and wait for the answer?
Does it speak the language you speak at home?
Can you see afterwards what it said?
Does it work without a screen?
Does it leave room for you to join in?
Whatever you choose, no toy replaces the people who talk with your child every day.
Try this:
when a toy talks, pause it and ask your child what it should say next.

content.text: This guide is for the parent standing in front of a toy that talks. It covers the part of the DPDP Act about children: what it says, when it starts, and what you can ask any company. It puts the law’s own words into plain language. It is not legal advice.
Who counts as a child?
Anyone under 18. The Act defines a child as “an individual who has not completed the age of eighteen years”.[^1] So everything below applies to a 3-year-old and a teenager alike.
Consent has to come from you

Section 9 says a company must get “verifiable consent of the parent” before it processes any personal data of a child.[^1] The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 add that the company must take “appropriate technical and organisational measures” to make sure it has that consent first.[^3]
So, once section 9 is in force, the yes has to come from you, the parent, before your child’s data is used.[^1]
What a company must not do

Section 9 sets two more limits. A company must not process personal data in a way that is “likely to cause any detrimental effect on the well-being of a child”.[^1] And it “shall not undertake tracking or behavioural monitoring of children or targeted advertising directed at children”.[^1]
The Rules list exceptions, such as a school tracking its pupils for their safety, or tracking a child’s real-time location to keep them safe.[^3]
Whichever toy you choose, ask the company how it gets your consent, and whether it tracks your child or shows them ads.
When does it start?

Not yet. The Act was published in August 2023, and the government is bringing it into force in stages.[^1][^2] Under its notification of November 2025, section 9 is due to come into force a year and a half later, in May 2027.[^2] The rule on a parent’s consent follows the same 18-month timetable.[^3]
Until then, the questions below are yours to ask, of any company.
What you can ask any company
Ask before any toy that listens comes home, and expect a plain answer:
How do you get my consent, and how do you check it is me?
Where is my child’s voice processed, and in which country?
Do you track my child, or show them ads?
Is my child’s data ever sold?
Can I read what my child said, and delete it myself?
How long do you keep it?
A vague answer is an answer.

posts.description: Screen-free activities for kids at home: ten-second setups, real jobs and quiet play for 3 to 7 year olds, including on the days you have to work.
posts.author: Kheelona

content.text: Below: ten-second setups, real jobs, ideas by age, and what to do on the days you have to work.
It is 4 pm, your call starts in ten minutes, and a small person is circling your desk asking what they can do. The tablet would solve it in four seconds.
Look at what the tablet offers: no setup, no grown-up needed, no way to get it wrong. An activity with the same three things has a fair chance against it.
Ten-second setups
Keep one low shelf of things that start at once and can stop anywhere:
a cup of water and a paintbrush, to “paint” an old slate
steel dabbas and their lids, to match up
old newspaper, to tear into the world’s biggest salad
a bedsheet over two chairs: a house until dinner
dough, a small rolling pin and a few cutters
a cardboard box, which can be a car, a cave and a shop before lunch
The plainer the thing, the more games it can be.
Give them a real job
To a 4-year-old, matching every sock in the basket is not a chore. It is a promotion.
Name the job and hand it over: “You’re in charge of the potatoes.” Washing vegetables, sorting spoons, watering the plants, guarding the dough while it rises. Let it be done their way.
Screen-free activities for a 3-year-old at home

Keep it big, simple and close to you: chunky crayons on a roll of paper taped to the floor, dough, stacking steel tumblers, pouring water between two cups over a basin, and dancing to a song you sing together.
Keep small things out of reach, and stay in the same room.
For a 5, 6 or 7-year-old: projects that last

Try projects that can run all afternoon and wait for tomorrow: a cardboard-box city, a treasure hunt with picture clues, a comic about the family cat, a shop with price tags they draw or write themselves.
Ask them to explain it to you at dinner. The telling is half the fun.
Quiet time: a story instead of a show
Some moments call for sitting still: after lunch, before bed, at the end of a long day.

For three and four year olds, the World Health Organization says screen time spent sitting and watching should be no more than an hour a day, and less is better. When children are sitting still, it encourages “reading and storytelling with a caregiver”.[^1]
Try this:
read a picture book once, then hand it over and let your child tell it back to you from the pictures.
On the days you have to work
For the stretches you can’t be interrupted, pick a quiet activity and set it up in the room where you work: water and a brush, dough, crayons on a roll of paper.
Save the ones that talk (a story played aloud, a grandparent on a voice call) for the stretches when you can listen with half an ear.
Kheelu

is one more screen-free option for those stretches: a plush toy for ages 3 to 7 that answers your child, then asks a question back. It is not a toy for children under 3. If your child is 3, keep a grown-up nearby while they play.
Most of this page needs no technology at all: a shelf, a basket of socks, a cardboard box.

posts.title: Does a three-year-old need an AI tutor?
posts.description: Does a 3-year-old need an AI tutor? No. What help at 3 looks like, what the WHO and IAP say about screens, and what to look for instead.
posts.author: Apoorva Sahu
posts.heroAlt: A little girl in a red polka-dot frock, tongue out in concentration, scribbling with an orange crayon at a low table.

content.text: What does help look like at 3?
A tutor, in the usual sense, helps a child keep up with school: homework, practice, tests. A 3-year-old doesn’t need any of those. What they have is questions.

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth “serve and return” exchanges between a young child and a caring adult help build and strengthen neural connections in the child’s brain. They also support the early language and social skills that later, more complex thinking builds on.[^1]
At 3, the serve is often a question. A good return answers it, then asks one back:
Your child:
Why is the dosa round?
You:
Because we spread the batter round and round. What shape would you make?
Your child:
A star!
You:
How would we flip a star?
Four turns, and your child did half the thinking. That is what help looks like at 3: a patient grown-up who answers the fourth “why” as kindly as the first.
Try this:
after your child’s next “why”, answer in a sentence, then ask, “What do you think?” Count to five before you say more.
What about a tutoring app on a tablet?
A tutoring app on a phone or tablet is screen time.

For three and four year olds, the Indian Academy of Pediatrics says no more than an hour of screen time a day, for no more than 20 to 30 minutes at a time, always supervised by a caregiver.[^2] The World Health Organization’s limit for watching screens at this age is the same hour, and it adds that less is better.[^3]

That hour covers every screen in the day, so a tutoring app shares it with everything else. From five to ten, the IAP’s limit is under two hours a day, and it counts screen time for schoolwork too.[^2]
If a screen is part of your child’s day, sit with them and talk about what you see.
What about AI that does the thinking for them?

In a May 2026 commentary for the Brookings Institution, Rebecca Winthrop, who directs its Center for Universal Education, described one worry about children and AI as “cognitive stunting”: relying too heavily on AI “reduces children’s opportunities to engage in effortful thinking”.[^4]
She calls the evidence emerging, and none of the findings she reports is about children as young as 3.[^4]

Whatever that evidence shows in time, the habit is easy to keep at home: give your child time to think before anyone, or anything, gives the answer. That is the case for a question back. It hands the thinking to your child.
What to look for instead
If you are weighing an AI toy or app for a young child, look for these:
Talk, not taps: your child speaks and listens, with no screen to watch.
It answers, then asks your child something back.
It says when it doesn’t know, instead of guessing.
It can’t browse the open internet.
You can read every conversation.
What child-safety groups advise about AI toys at this age, and our answer, is in our guide to
what to look for in a safe AI toy
Kheelu

is built around the list above: a screen-free plush toy for ages 3 to 7 that answers your child, then asks a question back. It can’t browse the internet, it says when it doesn’t know, and you can read every conversation in the parent app. It is a toy, not a tutor, and it tells your child it’s a toy.
It is not a toy for children under 3, and if your child is 3, keep a grown-up nearby while they play.

content.text: Chances are nobody sat your child down to teach them “auto”, “gravy” or “cousin”. The words arrived anyway: from the kitchen, the market, the back seat and the family video call.
Here is what the research says about talk and words, and what you can do at home today.
What does the research say about talk and words?

In a 2018 study of 36 children aged 4 to 6, children who had more back-and-forth conversational turns with adults showed more activity in Broca’s area, a language region of the brain, while listening to a story. The number of adult words they heard showed no such link. Turns also predicted the children’s language scores once family income and parents’ education were taken into account.[^2]
In the study, a turn was an adult speaking and the child replying, or the other way round. The children were native English speakers, and the study shows a link, not cause and effect.[^2]

Its authors suggest encouraging parents to talk with their children in “more interactive, back-and-forth conversation”.[^2] With a new word, one way to do that: say it, then give your child a reason to use it.
Everyday ways to build your child’s vocabulary
Use your real words: “enormous” and “delicious”, not only “big” and “nice”.
Explain a new word in the same breath: “The dal is boiling. See the bubbles?”
Name what your child points at, then wait for them to try the word.
Hand a new word back as a question: “It was enormous? How enormous?”
Read together, and talk about the pictures as well as the words.
Use a new word again over the next few days, somewhere new.
At meals, ask your child what they think, and let them finish.
None of this needs flashcards or a worksheet. It needs talk, a pause, and someone who listens to the answer.
Try this:
pick one new word from your day, like “drizzle” or “crowded”, and use it at dinner, at bath time and at bedtime.
Any language counts

Counting your child’s vocabulary? Count every language. A bilingual child may split their words across two languages. Counted together, the total should be about the same as for a child of the same age learning one language.[^1] Words collected in Telugu or Bangla count towards that total.[^1]
A strong model in any language also helps build a foundation for learning others.[^3] So keep talking in the languages you know best, every day.
For more on two languages at home, read
Raising a bilingual child in India
When should you ask your doctor?

Every child is different. As a general guide, if your child is 3 or older and other people still can’t understand them most of the time, or they lose words they used to have, talk to your paediatrician.[^4]

content.text: Your child asks why the moon follows the car. You answer, and before you’ve finished, the next question is on its way: “Then why doesn’t it follow the bus?”
Your child served. You returned. They served again. It happens all day: at breakfast, in the auto, at bath time.
What does the research say?

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child also calls serve and return, the back-and-forth between young children and the significant adults in their lives, “one of the most essential experiences in shaping the architecture of the developing brain”.[^2]

In a 2018 study of 36 children aged 4 to 6, children who had more back-and-forth conversational turns with adults showed more activity in Broca’s area, a language region of the brain, while listening to a story. The number of adult words they heard showed no such link. Turns also predicted the children’s language scores once family income and parents’ education were taken into account.[^3]
The study shows a link, not cause and effect.[^3] In the study, a turn was an adult speaking and the child replying, or the other way round.[^3] A turn needs both of you.
What does it look like at home?
At breakfast.
Your child holds up a half-eaten dosa: “It’s a moon!” You: “A half moon. What else on your plate is round?”
In the auto.
“Why is he honking?” You: “What do you think?” Wait for the answer, then add one thing you know.
At bath time.
Your child pours water from cup to cup. You: “Full. Now empty.” They say it back, and you wait for what comes next.
At bedtime.
Before you turn the page: “What do you think she’ll do?”
You can do it anywhere: answer your child, then ask one back.
Three habits that keep it going
Notice the serve. It can be a point, a question or a tug at your sleeve. Turn towards it when you can.
Wait. Give your child time to take their turn before you take yours.
Put your phone face down while you talk.
Who can return a serve?

Anyone who cares for your child. Harvard’s Center describes this back-and-forth as a relationship “between children and their parents and other caregivers in the family or community”.[^4] In your home, that might be a long list: Nani, Dada, an older cousin, the auntie next door.

Each of them can talk in the language they know best. ASHA, the US association of speech and hearing professionals, says a strong model in any language helps build a foundation for learning others.[^5]
No toy or screen replaces the people who talk with your child every day.

content.text: That hour is a ceiling, not a target.
Below: what changes at each age up to 7, and what to do when the evening gets hard.
How much screen time for a 4-year-old?

The same hour. The WHO and the IAP set it for four year olds too.[^1][^2] The American Academy of Pediatrics sets no more than an hour a day of high-quality programmes for children aged two to five, watched together.[^3]
For three and four year olds, the IAP adds two details: no more than 20 to 30 minutes at a time, and a grown-up always supervising.[^2]
How much screen time for a 5-year-old?
Under two hours a day, says the IAP, from 5 until 10, and that includes time on a screen for homework. Less is better.[^2] The WHO’s guideline stops at 4.[^1]
How much screen time at 6 and 7?

The IAP’s limit of under two hours a day still applies, homework included.[^2] The AAP’s advice for children aged 5 to 18 sets no fixed number of hours: it asks families to place consistent limits on time and on the kinds of media used.[^4]
Agree the limit with your child, keep it the same every day, and keep screens from crowding out sleep and play.
What if your child watches more than that?
You are not alone. Across 10 studies from India, covering 2,857 children under five, children averaged about 2.2 hours of screen time a day. That is more than the guidelines advise.[^5]
Cut back a little at a time, and have something ready to fill the gap. Our seven-day plan,
The gentle way off the phone
, shows one way to do it.
What the hour leaves room for

The AAP says the one-hour limit for young children is there to leave them “ample time to engage in other activities important to their health and development”.[^3] And when a young child is sitting still, the WHO encourages reading and storytelling with a caregiver.[^1]
So look at the whole day, not just the minutes. Is there room for talking, playing, moving about and sleep?
Does it matter what they watch?

Yes. The AAP says well-designed programmes “can improve cognitive, literacy, and social outcomes for children 3 to 5 years of age”.[^3] It also asks parents to avoid three things: fast-paced programmes (young children do not understand them as well), apps with lots of distracting content, and anything violent.[^3]
And it asks parents to watch with their children and help them understand what they are seeing.[^3]
Try this:
after an episode, ask your child to tell you what happened, and which part they liked best.
What about meals and bedtime?

For children under five, the IAP and the AAP both say no screens at meals and none in the hour before sleep.[^2][^3] The AAP also asks families to keep bedrooms screen-free.[^3] The IAP adds car, bus and train journeys to the screen-free list.[^2]
If your evening wind-down leans on a screen, move the screen earlier and put a bath, a story or a song in its place.
What do you do at 6 pm?
Knowing the number does not cook dinner. A few habits worth trying:
Decide when screen time ends before it starts, and tell your child.
End at a natural break, such as the end of an episode, not halfway through.
Put something your child enjoys straight after it, so the end is also a start.
Keep the screen in a room you share, not the bedroom.
Sit with them for a few minutes of it, and talk about what you see.

content.text: How was school? “Fine.” What did you do? “Nothing.” Two questions in, the conversation is over, and the child who once told you about every ant on the footpath now answers in one word.
A whole day is a lot to sum up, and “fine” does the job. So ask about a smaller piece of it.
Conversation starters for after school
Ask about one small, real moment instead of the whole day:
Who made you laugh today?
What was the best thing in your tiffin? And the worst?
Who did you sit next to? What did you talk about?
What was the hardest thing you did today?
What did you play outside? Who won?
On a day at home: “What did you and Nani see at the market?”
One question a day is plenty. Keep the rest for tomorrow.
Go first, then wait
Start with your own answer: “The worst thing in my lunch today was cold upma. What was yours?” Now your child knows the kind of answer you mean.
Then wait. Count to five in your head before you ask again or answer for them. It will feel long. Wait anyway.
Follow up on whatever comes back
Whatever your child says, take it one step further, out of curiosity, not as a quiz: “He fell off the bench? What did your teacher do? And then?”

In a 2018 study of 36 children aged 4 to 6, children who had more back-and-forth conversational turns with adults showed more activity in Broca’s area, a language region of the brain, while listening to a story. The number of adult words they heard showed no such link. The study shows a link, not cause and effect.[^2]

In the study, a turn was an adult speaking and the child replying, or the other way round.[^2] Its authors suggest encouraging parents to talk with their children in “more interactive, back-and-forth conversation”.[^2] Every follow-up is one more turn.
Games that get a child talking
In each of these, your child has to talk to take their turn.
Describe it, don’t point: “I spy something yellow that you peel before you eat it.” Then swap.
Play shop. Your child runs it, and you keep asking: “Do you have a smaller one? How much is it?”
Read a picture book together, and pause once or twice to ask what your child thinks will happen next.
Make up a story in turns: you say one line, your child says the next.
Sing a rhyme and stop before the last word, so your child can fill it in.
On a call with a grandparent, let your child tell one thing from their day.

content.text: The word “educational” on a box says little about the toy inside. A shape sorter is educational. So is a tablet full of phonics videos. They are not the same purchase.
A better question: what is my 3-year-old working on right now, and does this toy help or get in the way? Here is that list, skill by skill.
What is a 3-year-old working on?
India’s National Education Policy 2020 treats ages 3 to 8 as the Foundational Stage: three years of Anganwadi or pre-school, then Grades 1 and 2.[^2]

For these early years, it describes learning that is “play-based, activity-based, and inquiry-based”, covering languages, numbers and counting, colours and shapes, puzzles, drawing, craft, drama and puppetry, music and movement.[^3]
It is written for Anganwadis and pre-schools, not for toy shops. Here is what those kinds of play look like at home, skill by skill.
Language: does the toy make a turn?

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth “serve and return” exchanges between a young child and a caring adult help build and strengthen neural connections in the child’s brain. They also support the early language and social skills that later, more complex thinking builds on.[^1]

In a 2018 study of 36 children aged 4 to 6, children who had more back-and-forth conversational turns with adults showed more activity in Broca’s area, a language region of the brain, while listening to a story. The number of adult words they heard showed no such link. The study shows a link, not cause and effect.[^4]

So the test for a language toy is simple: does it make a turn? A picture book you read together makes plenty. A puppet makes as many as you have patience for. A toy that plays a recorded sentence at the press of a button can’t answer back, however many words the sentence has.
Try this:
when you read together, pause once or twice and ask what your child thinks will happen next.
Taking turns: games with a “your go, my go” rhythm

Look for games where your child has to wait, watch and then go: simple board games with two rules, picture matching, rolling a ball back and forth. Play them together and say the turns out loud: “My go. Now yours.”
Pretend play: props that leave the story to your child

A cardboard kitchen, a doctor set, a box of mismatched figures. Open props let your child decide who is cooking and what is wrong with teddy. A toy kitchen that plays its own sounds and names its own characters decides some of that for them.

content.text: Hands: plain things do the job
Threading beads, stacking cups, dough, chunky crayons, tongs and a bowl of pom-poms. None of them needs a battery or a screen.
Numbers: count real things together
Count spoons at dinner, steps to the door, autos at the signal. Ask, “Which pile has more?” Any toy with parts you can count will do.
Brain development toys for a 3-year-old: what the label means
The words “brain development” on a box prove nothing on their own. What matters is whether a toy gets your child trying, asking and explaining, and whether you talk together while they play.

Harvard’s centre describes the same back-and-forth from infancy: exchanges between a young child and a caring adult that help build and strengthen the connections in the child’s brain.[^1] So for a younger child the rule is the same: fewer toys that perform, more time playing and talking together.
What about screens?
For three and four year olds, the World Health Organization and the Indian Academy of Pediatrics both say no more than an hour of screen time a day, and less is better.[^5][^6]
The American Academy of Pediatrics asks parents to watch with their children, help them understand what they are seeing, and switch screens off an hour before bedtime.[^7]
When your child does watch, sit with them and talk about it.
A short rule for the toy shop
Check the age on the box.
Prefer toys that wait for your child over toys that perform at them.
Prefer open ends over scripts.
Prefer anything that makes a turn.

content.text: You may know this moment. You ask something in Kannada, and your child answers in English. Part of you is proud. Part of you wonders whether the home language is slipping away.
Under it sits an older worry: are two languages too much for a young child? Here is what the research says, and what keeps a home language going.
Does a second language confuse or delay a young child?

No. A 2013 review of the research, written for parents by two researchers who study bilingual infants and children, says it plainly: bilingual children are not more likely than monolingual children to have difficulties with language, to show delays in learning, or to be diagnosed with a language disorder.[^3]

They may know fewer words in each language on its own. Count the ideas they have a word for in either language, counting “paani” and “water” once, and the total is about the same as for a child growing up with one language.[^3] Most of the studies it draws on were done in North America and Europe.[^3]

The American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association say the same in their advice for parents: “Speech or language problems are not caused by learning multiple languages.”[^1]
Is mixing two languages a problem?

No. Mixing words or grammar from two languages in one sentence is normal, and it isn’t confusion.[^1] Usually by age 3, children learning more than one language can keep them apart, and use the one that suits the person they’re talking to.[^1]
So when your child answers your Tamil in English, answer back in Tamil, warmly.
Is the home language in the way of English?
No. ASHA, the US association of speech and hearing professionals, says in its guidance for clinicians that a strong model in any language helps build a foundation for learning others.[^2]

Jim Cummins, a University of Toronto researcher on bilingual education, argues that concepts learned in the mother tongue carry over to a second language. A child who can tell the time in one language, he writes, does not need to re-learn the concept in another, only the new labels for it.[^4] He was writing about children at school.[^4]
What does India’s education policy say?

India’s National Education Policy 2020 says that, wherever possible, children should be taught in their home language, mother tongue, or local or regional language until at least Grade 5, and preferably till Grade 8 and beyond.[^5] The policy gives its reason in the same paragraph: young children “learn and grasp nontrivial concepts more quickly in their home language/mother tongue”.[^5]
It is a policy for schools, followed wherever possible, not a law.
What keeps a home language alive?
Give it jobs: the songs, the food words, the jokes and the stories one grandparent tells best.
Speak it without apology, at home and outside.
When your child answers in English, reply in your language, warmly.
Read in it, even if the books take some finding.
Keep calls with grandparents and cousins in their language.
Let it carry the good moments, not only “eat your food” and “time for bed”.
Try this:
this week, ask a grandparent to tell your child one story in the home language, on a call or in person.
Who speaks what, day to day?

Families do this in different ways: one language for each parent, one language at home and English at school, or grandparents who keep the home language going. Pick a pattern your household can keep, and change it when life changes.

content.text: Take the tablet away and the first thing you notice is the noise. Not the TV kind. The good kind: questions, made-up songs, a running commentary on the ants.
You may worry that screen-free means a quieter, duller childhood. It doesn’t have to. A screen mostly asks a child to watch. Play asks them to do things, and talk asks them to answer.
What does a childhood full of talk look like?
It sounds like turns: your child says something, you answer, they answer back.

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth “serve and return” exchanges between a young child and a caring adult help build and strengthen neural connections in the child’s brain. They also support the early language and social skills that later, more complex thinking builds on.[^1]
At home, that comes from small habits, not a curriculum:
Say what you’re doing while you cook: “Onions first. Now the tomatoes. Smell that?”
Ask questions with no wrong answer: “What would the cat say if it could talk?”
Let the silly voice read the bedtime story.
Now and then, answer a question with a question: “Why do you think the moon follows the car?”
Leave gaps in songs for your child to fill.
Leave room for boredom
When your child says “I’m bored”, wait a few minutes before you fix it. The floor may become lava. The sofa may become a ship.
Screen-free does not mean silent, and it does not mean joyless. Often it means the sound in your home is your child thinking out loud.
How do you choose screen-free toys?
Ask one question in the shop: what will my child do with this, and what will they say?
Blocks and boxes: they build, then tell you what it is.
Pretend-play sets: someone has to be the doctor, and someone has to say what’s wrong with teddy.
Puppets: a second voice for a quiet child.
Picture books: read together, then let them tell it back.
Simple board games: “My go. Now yours.”
A toy that plays the same recorded sentence at every press makes noise, but it can’t answer back.
Looking for a screen-free gift?

Choose something your child can do, build or say, rather than watch: a box of blocks, a puppet, a book you’ll read together, crayons with a roll of paper. Then play with it together, the first time at least.
Story box or a toy that talks back?
They do different jobs. A story box or audio player plays stories your child listens to. A toy that talks back holds a conversation: your child asks, it answers, then it asks a question back.
Both are screen-free. Choose by what you want more of at home: listening, or talking.

content.text: One common tip is missing on purpose: the two-minute warning. More on that below.
The video ends. You say that’s enough for today. And a child who sat quietly for half an hour is suddenly on the floor in tears.
If this is your house some evenings, you are not alone.
Why the meltdown comes at the off switch

Screen time tantrums are common enough that researchers have studied them: a 2016 University of Washington study of families with children aged 1 to 5 found that “transitioning away from screens is often painful”.[^1]
Think about what the off switch asks of a young child: to stop something they enjoy, right now, at a moment they did not choose. That is hard at any age.

It does not happen every evening, though. The study’s senior author said that most of the time these transitions “actually go pretty smoothly”, even if parents find that hard to see.[^2] It is the hard evenings that stay with you.
What makes taking the phone away easier?
How the screen ends makes a difference. In the same study, routines and stopping at a natural break made the switch easier.[^2]

One well-meant habit made it harder: children given a two-minute warning by their parents were more upset when the screen went away.[^2] That is one study, so watch your own child. If the countdown sets off the storm, drop it.
How to make switching off boring
Boring is the goal: an ending so routine that there is nothing to fight about.
Agree the plan out loud before the screen goes on: “One episode, then we water the plants.”
Stop at the end of an episode or a song, never halfway through.
Turn off autoplay, so the next episode does not start on its own.
Keep the same order every day, so the ending is no surprise.
Have something ready for their hands the moment the screen goes dark: dough, crayons, a job in the kitchen.
If tears come, stay close, stay calm and keep to what you said.

What is the worry about children and AI?

In a May 2026 commentary for the Brookings Institution, Rebecca Winthrop, who directs its Center for Universal Education, described one worry about children and AI as “cognitive stunting”: relying too heavily on AI “reduces children’s opportunities to engage in effortful thinking”.[^2] She points to children’s wide use of “general-purpose chatbots and AI companions not designed for learning”, and calls the evidence early.[^2]
Give your child time to think before anyone, or anything, gives the answer.
What do child-safety groups advise?
In November 2025 Fairplay, a children’s advocacy group, published an advisory signed by more than 150 experts and organisations telling parents not to buy AI toys that season.[^3]

In January 2026, Common Sense Media advised parents not to give AI toys, which it describes as “smart toys with voice-based interactions”, to children aged 5 and under, and to use extreme caution before buying them for children aged 6 to 12.[^1] When it tested three AI toys, it rated 27% of their replies as not appropriate for kids. It also raised concerns about toys designed to create emotional attachment, the data they collect and how reliably they work.[^4]
Common Sense Media also says children aged 5 and under “cannot reliably distinguish AI from real people”.[^4]
Most of these concerns are about how a toy is built, and those you can check. The age advice is about young children themselves, and only you can weigh it for yours.
What does the research say young children need?

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth “serve and return” exchanges between a young child and a caring adult help build and strengthen neural connections in the child’s brain. They also support the early language and social skills that later, more complex thinking builds on.[^5]

In a US study of 90 children aged between 3 and 6, children asked about a story by an adult researcher gave longer answers, using more different words, than children asked the same questions by a smart speaker. Both groups answered about equally accurately.[^6]
You can do it anywhere: answer your child, then ask one back. And the test for any AI near a young child is simple: does it leave more room for that back-and-forth with you, or less?

Ask the same four questions of every maker, us included.
Can it reach the open internet?
Is every reply checked for your child’s age, and can the maker say how?
Can you read every conversation, and how do you delete it?
Does it talk with your child, in questions and turns, or perform at them?
A maker who answers all four plainly is worth a closer look. For us, AI near a young child is not a simple yes or no. It is a question of who built it, and why.

content.text: At a birthday party, another child is narrating a whole film, and yours points and says “come”. Is that fine? Or is it something?
Here is what varies between children, what deserves a professional look, and what helps at home either way.
What varies from child to child?
The milestones from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) sit at the age by which at least 3 in 4 children reach each one.[^3] So they describe most children, not every child.
The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) says its own milestone chart “is not a screening or diagnostic tool”. It is meant to start a conversation with your child’s doctor.[^5]
And watch your child at home, where they are most at ease, not only at a party.
Two languages at home? Count every word

Asked whether using more than one language can cause a speech or language disorder, the American Academy of Pediatrics and ASHA answer no: “Speech or language problems are not caused by learning multiple languages.”[^6]

A child learning two languages may split their words across them. Counted together, the total should be about the same as for a child of the same age learning one language.[^6] So count the words in every language your child uses, and keep them all going.
When is it worth a professional look?
Talk to your child’s doctor if:
at 3, your child doesn’t yet put two or more words together, with one action word, like “Doggie run”;[^2]
at 3, your child doesn’t yet keep up a short conversation with you, of at least two back-and-forth exchanges;[^4]
at 3, other people still can’t understand your child most of the time;[^4]
by 4, your child doesn’t yet say sentences of four or more words;[^1]
by 4, people can’t yet understand most of what your child says;[^7]
at any age, your child loses words or skills they used to have.[^4]
These are US guides, and every child is different. Missing one is a reason to ask, not a diagnosis.

The CDC suggests you share your concerns with your child’s doctor and ask about developmental screening.[^4] ASHA suggests an assessment by an audiologist, who checks hearing, or a speech-language pathologist if a child misses many of the milestones for their age.[^7]
If your gut says ask, ask.
What helps at home, either way

Whatever the milestones say, keep the back-and-forth going. Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth exchanges between a young child and a caring adult support early language and social skills.[^8]
Say what you’re doing while you do it, in short sentences: “Shoes on. This foot. Now that one.”
Offer a choice instead of a yes-or-no question: “Idli or dosa?” A choice asks for a word.
When your child says a word, say it back with one more: “Bus.” “Big bus.”
After you ask, wait. Count to five in your head before you help.
Read the same book again, and stop before a word your child knows.
Sing rhymes and leave the last word for your child.
Turn off the TV in the background while you talk and play.
None of this needs a purchase. Grandparents, cousins and older children can all take a turn.

content.text: Few silences are louder than a 3-year-old who says less than the cousins. The family group chat fills with advice, most of it confident and some of it wrong.
Here is what public guidance says, and what you can do at home today.
When should you ask a professional?
As a general guide, talk to your child’s doctor if:
at 3, other people still can’t understand your child most of the time;[^1]
at 3, your child doesn’t yet keep up a short conversation with you, of at least two back-and-forth exchanges;[^1]
by 4, people can’t yet understand most of what your child says;[^2]
at any age, your child loses words or skills they used to have.[^1]
These are US guides, and every child is different. Missing one is a reason to ask, not a diagnosis.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggest you talk with your child’s doctor, share your concerns and ask about developmental screening.[^1] ASHA, the US association of speech and hearing professionals, suggests an assessment by an audiologist or a speech-language pathologist if a child misses many of the milestones for their age.[^2]
If your gut says ask, ask.
What does the research say helps?

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth “serve and return” exchanges between a young child and a caring adult help build and strengthen neural connections in the child’s brain. They also support the early language and social skills that later, more complex thinking builds on.[^3]

In a 2018 study of 36 children aged 4 to 6, children who had more back-and-forth conversational turns with adults showed more activity in Broca’s area, a language region of the brain, while listening to a story. The number of adult words they heard showed no such link.[^4] The children were typically developing, not late talkers, and the study shows a link, not cause and effect.[^4]

Its authors suggest encouraging parents to talk with their children in “more interactive, back-and-forth conversation”.[^4] A turn can be tiny: your child points, you name the thing, they try the word, you smile and add one more.
What helps at home, every day
Talk about what you’re doing, in short sentences: “The dal is boiling. Now the cooker. One whistle, two.”
After you ask something, wait longer than feels natural. Count to five in your head.
Offer choices out loud: “The red cup or the blue cup?” A choice asks for a word.
Answer every try as if it were a full sentence, then add one word: “Ball? Yes, a big ball.”
Read the same book again, and pause before a word your child knows so they can say it.
Sing together, and leave gaps for your child to fill.
Turn off the TV in the background while you play and talk.
None of this needs a programme or a purchase. It needs turns, and anyone who loves your child can give them: parents, grandparents, cousins, the auntie next door.
Two myths worth dropping
Myth 1: a second home language causes speech delay.

Asked whether using more than one language can cause a speech or language disorder, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association answer no: “Speech or language problems are not caused by learning multiple languages.”[^5] A bilingual child may split their words across two languages. Counted together, the total should be about the same as for a child of the same age learning one language.[^5] And a strong model in any language helps build a foundation for learning others.[^6] Keep both languages.
Myth 2: a talking toy will teach your child to talk.
A toy that plays recorded phrases or repeats your child’s words gives them nothing new to answer. No toy replaces the people who talk with your child every day.

content.text: Here it is as a seven-day plan. Start on any day of the week.
Why replace before you remove?
Nobody plans for their 4-year-old to find the video app faster than they can. It happens one busy evening at a time.
The phone came in because it solved something: a work call, a bored child, the queue at the clinic. Take it away without replacing what it did, and the gap turns into a fight.
So this plan replaces first and removes second.
What are you aiming for?

The Indian Academy of Pediatrics says at most one hour of supervised screen time a day from two to five. From five to ten, it says less than two hours a day, including screens used for homework. For both ages, it adds: “the lesser, the better”.[^1]
For children aged two to five, it also says not to use screens during meals, within an hour before sleep, or “during surface travel”: in the car, on the bus, on the train.[^1]
The American Academy of Pediatrics asks families of young children to keep bedrooms, mealtimes and playtime together screen-free, for parents as well as children.[^2]
You don’t need to get there this week. The plan starts with one slot. For the numbers age by age, read
How much screen time is okay for a young child?
Days 1 and 2: notice when the phone comes out
Change nothing yet. Notice when the phone appears: the morning rush, the cooking hour, the car, the queue at the clinic.
Each one is a job the phone was hired to do. Write them down. That list is your plan for the week.
Days 3 and 4: replace the easiest slot

Pick the slot where the stakes are lowest. Fill it with something that talks back or keeps hands busy. A story, told or played aloud, in your home language. A grandparent on a voice call. A puzzle you started together at breakfast, waiting on the table.
Leave the hard slots alone for now. One calm win is worth more than three fights.
Need more ideas for the slot? Try
Busy hands, no screens
Days 5 and 6: shrink the rest, don’t snatch
In the slots that are left, end the screen at a natural break: the end of an episode, not the middle of a scene.
Then land it somewhere: a job, a snack, a spot-the-crow contest at the window. Have the next thing ready before the screen goes dark.
Try this:
before the screen goes on, say where it will land: “One episode, then we water the plants.”
If switching off is the hard part, read
Screen time and tantrums
Day 7: say the new rules out loud
Tell your child what changed, in the language you speak at home: mornings are for songs now, the car is for spotting autos, dinner is for talking.

Say it the same way every time, so it sounds like a rule, not a mood. And keep the rule yourself: at meals and at playtime together, the American Academy of Pediatrics suggests parents set their phones to “do not disturb”.[^2]
Week 2: expect a wobble
Some days will slip: a long journey, a sick day, a deadline. It happens. Go back to your list and pick up where you stopped.
Look at what your slots needed in the end: something to do, and someone to talk to, whether that is you, a grandparent or a sibling.

content.text: This page skips the flashcards. What the sources below point to is older and plainer: talk, sleep, calm and play. Here is each one, and how to get more of it at home.
Conversation: the back-and-forth kind

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child calls “serve and return”, the back and forth between young children and the significant adults in their lives, “one of the most essential experiences in shaping the architecture of the developing brain”.[^2] When your child reaches out with a sound, a look or a gesture and you respond, that is serve and return.[^2] By 3, that reaching out is often a question or a story.

In a 2018 study of 36 children aged 4 to 6, children who had more back-and-forth conversational turns with adults showed more activity in Broca’s area, a language region of the brain, while listening to a story. The number of adult words they heard showed no such link. The study shows a link, not cause and effect.[^3]
So aim for turns, not just words. A few ways to get more of them:
Answer a question, then ask one back: “What do you think?”
Give your child time to answer before you fill the silence.
Talk about what you’re doing while you cook, walk or fold the washing, and leave gaps for your child to add something.
At bedtime, ask about the best and the hardest part of the day, and hear the whole answer.
Sleep: more of it than you might think

Children aged 3 to 5 need 10 to 13 hours of sleep in every 24, naps included, and children aged 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours. Getting the recommended hours regularly goes with better attention, behaviour, learning and memory.[^4]
In one small US study, preschoolers remembered more of a memory game they had learnt that morning after a nap than after staying awake.[^5]
So protect bedtime. Keep it about the same most nights, keep the last hour before it screen-free, and end the day with a story or a chat.
Calm: a grown-up who steadies the hard days

Not all stress is bad. But serious, ongoing adversity, such as abuse, neglect, violence or the strain of family hardship, can disrupt how a young child’s brain develops when no caring adult is there to buffer it. Scientists call this toxic stress.[^6] Supportive relationships with caring adults help protect against it.[^6]
So calm does not mean a silent house, or a child who never cries. It means a grown-up who notices, comforts and stays. On a hard day, that comes first.
Play: time with nothing planned
India’s National Education Policy 2020 describes good early learning as “play-based, activity-based, and inquiry-based”.[^7]

At home, that can be an afternoon with nothing on the calendar and a few open things within reach: blocks, a cardboard box, a dupatta that can be a cape or a river. Let your child decide what the game is, and join in when you’re invited.
The dinner-table test
A simple test for any toy, app or class: after ten minutes with it, does your child have something to tell you? Try it on what is already in your home: the blocks, the picture books, the cartoons.

content.text: None of it needs a class or a kit. Here is what is being built, and the three ordinary things that fill these years well.
What happens in a young child’s brain?

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child estimates that more than a million new connections form in the brain every second in the first few years of life.[^1] The early years are the most active period for building those connections, but new connections can form throughout life.[^1]

India’s National Curriculum Framework for the Foundational Stage says brain development is most rapid in the first eight years of a child’s life.[^3] So if your child is between 3 and 7, they are still inside those years.
Both describe how busy these years are. Neither is a deadline.
Talk: answer, then ask one back

Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child says back-and-forth “serve and return” exchanges between a young child and a caring adult help build and strengthen neural connections in the child’s brain. They also support the early language and social skills that later, more complex thinking builds on.[^2]
Between 3 and 7, a serve is often a question, a story or a complaint about a sibling. Your return is your attention and a reply. Try ending it with a question back, then wait.
For more ways to do this every day, read our guide to
what actually builds a sharp brain
Play, and plenty of it

India’s National Education Policy 2020 treats ages 3 to 8 as the Foundational Stage of school education: three years of Anganwadi or pre-school, then Grades 1 and 2.[^4] It describes those five years as “flexible, multilevel, play/activity-based learning”.[^4]
At home, play needs very little: a pretend shop, a cardboard box that becomes a bus, a tower built only to be knocked down. Let your child lead, and join in when you’re asked.
Sleep, the part that’s easiest to cut
Children aged 3 to 5 need 10 to 13 hours of sleep in every 24, naps included, and children aged 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours.[^5]
Late dinners, family functions and screens all eat into it. So keep bedtime steady, most nights.
What these years don’t need
A packed timetable. Flashcards before breakfast. The worry that you have already missed something.
What fills these years well is ordinary: talk, play and sleep, most days, with the people who love your child.
Kheelu

is built around the first of those: a screen-free plush toy for ages 3 to 7 that answers your child, then asks a question back. No toy replaces the people who talk with your child every day, ours included.
It is not a toy for children under 3, and if your child is 3, keep a grown-up nearby while they play.
